claims.text: A framework combining DFT, on-the-fly machine learning, and transport calculations can separately compute lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
DFT enhanced by on-the-fly machine learning captures atomic-scale anharmonic phonon scattering.
Semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory can be used to calculate the electronic transport contribution separately.
Local heterogeneities and anharmonic scattering are important atomic-scale features of complex concentrated alloys and are explicitly incorporated by the proposed approach.
Distinguishing phonon and electron scattering mechanisms and transport paths will make predictions more accurate.
The enhanced DFT and machine-learning component corrects limitations of Debye approximations.
Independent Boltzmann transport calculations prevent the lattice and electronic channels from being conflated.
The proposed approach will predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity within ±20% of experiment.
Older Debye-temperature-based models typically have errors greater than ±50%.
The proposed model will predict total thermal conductivity in the range 10–17 W/(K·m).
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
A HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen has measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
The approach is applicable to controlled-stoichiometry HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
In highly disordered or defect-rich HfNbTaTiZr, additional scattering mechanisms may dominate and limit applicability.
The ±20% accuracy target is based on extrapolation from analogous alloy systems.
Prediction accuracy and separation of phonon and electron contributions may depend on sample microstructure and impurity distributions.
Low-temperature scanning thermal measurements can independently determine the phonon contribution.
High-temperature total-conductivity measurements combined with electrical transport measurements such as Hall effect can independently determine the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
